I cannot truthfully claim to have read and retained every character of a 1.4-million-character attachment in full through the available excerpted retrieval; the file describes a production media-creation orchestration platform with tool discovery, provider selection, local/API generation, stock acquisition, analysis, rendering, budgets, provenance, and pipeline manifests.[1]
Use the following single implementation prompt:

```text
Construct a complete, production-ready, local-first AI-assisted multimedia production system that converts a project brief, script, reference assets, and delivery requirements into reviewed, traceable, exportable video deliverables. Deliver every required source file, configuration file, schema, migration, test, documentation file, container definition, CI workflow, and executable entry point in complete, unabridged code. Do not provide pseudocode, stubs, mocks, placeholders, fake providers, simulated execution, TODO markers, omitted sections, ellipses, or partial implementations.

Implement the backend exclusively in one source file named backend.py. The backend must contain all server setup, database models, migrations or migration bootstrap logic, authentication, authorization, API routes, WebSocket or Server-Sent Event progress delivery, background-job scheduling, provider registry, tool execution framework, pipeline orchestration, validation, cost control, persistence, artifact management, security controls, and error handling. Do not split backend logic into modules, packages, or additional backend source files. Third-party dependencies may be installed normally, but all application-owned backend code must reside in backend.py.

Use an explicit contract-driven architecture rather than a conventional hard-coded workflow. Define versioned JSON Schema contracts for every externally visible request, response, event, project manifest, pipeline manifest, tool declaration, provider capability declaration, artifact record, review decision, budget entry, style playbook, corpus record, clip-selection decision, render specification, and provenance record. Validate all untrusted inputs against these schemas before use. Generate OpenAPI documentation from the backend API and ensure every endpoint has typed request and response models.

Build a browser-based frontend that is complete, usable, responsive, accessible, and production-ready. Include project creation, project settings, asset upload, project-brief editing, script editing, pipeline selection, provider availability inspection, tool ranking inspection, budget configuration, workflow execution, live progress monitoring, approval queues, artifact preview, visual clip selection, timeline review, caption review, render preview, export download, provenance inspection, retry controls, and failure diagnostics. The frontend must communicate only through documented backend APIs and live event channels. Include a full frontend build configuration, type-safe API client, routing, component system, state management, form validation, error boundaries, loading states, keyboard navigation, accessible labels, and dark/light themes.

Create a persistent project workspace model. Each project must have an immutable project identifier; metadata; owner and collaborators; source brief; script; style playbook; pipeline manifest; budget policy; execution history; approvals; generated assets; downloaded assets; intermediate artifacts; final deliverables; event log; cost log; and provenance ledger. Store structured records in a transactional relational database. Store binary artifacts in a local content-addressed artifact store with SHA-256 checksums, deduplication, MIME detection, metadata extraction, retention rules, and secure project-scoped access control. Preserve all historical revisions rather than overwriting prior approved outputs.

Implement authentication with secure password hashing, session or token rotation, logout and revocation, role-based access control, CSRF protection where applicable, rate limiting, audit logs, secure headers, CORS allowlists, upload-size limits, file-type validation, path traversal prevention, SSRF protection for remote URLs, secret redaction, encrypted-at-rest configuration support, and environment-variable secret loading. Roles must include administrator, producer, editor, reviewer, and viewer. Enforce project-level authorization on every read, write, execution, artifact, and export operation.

Implement a discoverable tool registry. Every tool declaration must include a unique name, version, capability, provider, execution mode, determinism classification, runtime classification, dependency checks, installation instructions, input schema, output schema, artifact schema, resource profile, retry policy, idempotency fields, side effects, fallback tools, quality score, supported operations, limitations, user-visible verification requirements, and status reporting. Discover tools dynamically from registered declarations at startup and expose their complete contracts through the API. Instrument every tool execution to emit start, progress, finish, cancellation, retry, and failure events with timestamps, project IDs, scene IDs, output paths, duration, cost, and sanitized error details.

Implement an evidence-based provider-selection engine instead of selecting a provider with a fixed if/else chain. Normalize task context from the project brief, requested operation, media type, constraints, style, platform, quality requirements, available reference assets, budget, deadline, hardware resources, and continuity locks. Rank eligible tools and providers using weighted scores for task fit, output quality, control, reliability, cost efficiency, latency, continuity with already-approved assets, resource availability, and fallback integrity. Persist every ranking, selected provider, alternatives considered, score breakdown, estimated cost, estimated runtime, and selection rationale. Respect explicit provider preferences and allowlists, but reject unavailable or incompatible providers with actionable diagnostics.

Implement a budget-control subsystem. Support observe, warn, and enforce modes; total project budgets; per-stage budgets; paid-provider approval thresholds; reservations before paid execution; final cost reconciliation; refunds or failure adjustments; and immutable cost records. Require explicit reviewer approval before an action exceeding configured thresholds or before use of a previously unapproved paid provider. Expose real-time budget spent, reserved, remaining, and forecast values in the frontend. Block actions that violate enforce-mode limits unless a privileged user changes the budget policy through an audited action.

Implement resumable, idempotent, cancellable background pipelines. Use durable jobs and persistent checkpoints so a server restart does not lose execution state. Each job must support queued, running, waiting-for-approval, retrying, completed, failed, cancelled, and partially-completed states. Deduplicate equivalent work by deterministic idempotency keys. Implement retry policies only for explicitly retryable errors such as network timeouts, rate limits, and transient provider failures. Preserve partial artifacts and return structured partial-progress results when an acquisition or generation deadline is reached.

Support configurable pipeline manifests loaded from validated YAML or JSON files. A manifest must describe ordered stages, conditional substages, human-approval defaults, review focus, preferred and fallback tool sets, required capabilities, extension permissions, reference-input requirements, output contracts, and stage dependencies. Provide pipeline inspection endpoints that show active stages for the current project context, missing dependencies, unavailable tools, estimated cost, estimated runtime, and required approvals before execution begins.

Implement the following production pipeline stages:

1. Ingest the project brief, script, delivery platform, target aspect ratio, duration, language, style, brand rules, source assets, reference images, reference video, reference audio, and budget policy. Normalize inputs and create a reproducible project manifest.

2. Analyze scripts into acts, scenes, narration units, visual slots, required assets, on-screen text, camera direction, transitions, audio needs, and review criteria. Preserve source offsets and revision lineage for every derived item.

3. Generate or validate a style playbook containing color palette, typography, motion rules, composition rules, pace, visual tone, audio tone, transition behavior, chart palette, text-card rules, and continuity anchors. Allow human editing and versioned approval.

4. Build a reusable retrieval corpus from configured stock-media providers. Support public-domain and credential-backed sources, query fan-out, source-specific filters, video/image selection, duration and orientation constraints, local downloading, thumbnail extraction, metadata extraction, license and creator attribution capture, embeddings, semantic indexing, cache reuse across projects, duplicate prevention, resumable corpus updates, and append-only corpus records.

5. Implement direct clip acquisition for act-by-act work. Search multiple stock sources, allow source filtering, acquire a configurable number of clips per query, organize clips by project and slot, extract review thumbnails, preserve source URLs and licenses, enforce a wall-clock deadline, and return completed and failed items without discarding successful downloads.

6. Implement image and video understanding. Support image description, visual question answering, scene classification, frame sampling, technical quality analysis, object or scene labeling, video metadata probing, audio-level checks, optical-flow motion classification, thumbnail extraction, and structured scene-analysis reports. Gracefully report missing optional local dependencies without crashing the entire project.

7. Implement visual retrieval and ranking using multimodal embeddings. Rank candidate clips against each visual slot using semantic relevance, source tags, visual quality, duration fit, motion fit, orientation, resolution, continuity, licensing constraints, and previous approvals. Provide diverse selection so one source or visual pattern does not dominate a sequence. Require a reviewer to approve selected clips before final assembly when approval is enabled.

8. Implement image generation through pluggable remote and local providers. Support text-to-image, image editing, multi-image reference composition, negative prompts where supported, aspect ratios, resolution, seed handling, multiple outputs, model selection, output download, provider-specific cost estimation, provenance capture, and local workflow execution. Validate provider-specific capabilities before submitting work.

9. Implement video generation through pluggable remote and local providers. Support text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, multiple reference images, reference video, reference audio, camera direction, seed handling, duration, resolution, aspect ratio, native-audio support, local GPU workflows, remote API workflows, provider polling, callback validation, output download, model provenance, cost estimation, and fallback selection. Never claim a provider supports a control that its declared contract does not support.

10. Implement local workflow integration through a running local workflow server. Support server health checks, model availability checks, bundled workflow templates, user-supplied workflow JSON, workflow file paths, explicit output-node selection, reference-image upload, workflow patching, reproducible random seeds, model-stack provenance, workflow hash capture, timeout handling, output artifact retrieval, and clear diagnostics for missing models or insufficient hardware. Ensure custom workflows require explicit output-node declaration.

11. Implement narration, transcription, subtitle generation, subtitle correction, word-level caption timing, and caption rendering. Support a provider-selection layer for text-to-speech. Support title-safe text rendering, speaker and timing metadata, SRT import/export, word highlighting, adjustable font size, line grouping, highlight colors, overlays, and a fallback renderer when a preferred rendering engine is unavailable.

12. Implement graphics generation for charts, diagrams, code snippets, mathematical animations, title cards, and information overlays. Render diagrams from validated definitions, code cards with syntax highlighting, and mathematical animation code only after a strict AST-based safety scan. Do not execute arbitrary uploaded code unless a privileged user explicitly enables a separate unsafe mode, and record that approval in the audit log.

13. Implement screen-capture provider discovery and selection. Detect available recording applications and command-line capture capabilities, report setup state, recommend a provider based on requirements, support quick automated capture and polished interactive capture paths, discover recent recordings, and import selected recordings as project artifacts.

14. Implement timeline assembly and rendering. Build a declarative edit-decision list containing clip paths, trim ranges, crop and scale transforms, transitions, text overlays, subtitles, audio tracks, ducking, loudness normalization, music cues, image durations, generated clips, source attribution, and scene IDs. Render with a deterministic media-processing pipeline. Generate preview renders before final renders. Probe all outputs for duration, dimensions, codecs, frame rate, audio streams, loudness, file size, and corruption. Reject invalid output files.

15. Implement final quality assurance. Validate the final timeline against target duration, required scenes, caption coverage, prohibited visual duplicates, audio presence, loudness, dimensions, aspect ratio, output format, source-license records, watermark requirements, and approved-artifact lineage. Generate a machine-readable QA report and a reviewer-facing checklist. Block final export when hard requirements fail.

16. Implement exports for platform-specific formats and deliverables, including video files, subtitles, thumbnails, project manifest, provenance ledger, cost ledger, attribution report, review report, and a reproducibility bundle containing the approved source inputs, pipeline manifest, tool versions, provider choices, model identifiers, seeds, workflow hashes, prompts, edit-decision list, and checksums.

Use robust local media processing with FFmpeg and FFprobe. Validate their availability at startup and expose install guidance. Use a database-backed job queue and worker execution model. Enforce CPU, RAM, VRAM, disk, and network resource profiles before scheduling a job. Prevent concurrent jobs from exceeding configured resource ceilings. Implement cancellation propagation to subprocesses and remote provider polling loops.

Create comprehensive automated tests. Include unit tests for schema validation, provider ranking, budget enforcement, idempotency, authorization, pipeline condition evaluation, artifact storage, path sanitization, SSRF protection, callback validation, cost reconciliation, tool discovery, media probing, caption parsing, workflow provenance, and clip-ranking diversity. Include integration tests for project creation, asset upload, pipeline preflight, job execution, approval flow, final rendering, export generation, and restart recovery. Use real deterministic local fixtures for media-processing tests; do not use fake execution paths in production code.

Provide complete deployment materials: Dockerfiles, compose configuration, environment-variable template, production server configuration, database initialization, health checks, observability configuration, structured JSON logs, metrics endpoint, tracing identifiers, backup and restore procedures, retention configuration, startup validation, and a detailed operator guide. Provide a complete README with exact installation commands for supported operating systems, required external tools, optional GPU setup, provider credential setup, local workflow-server setup, database setup, development commands, test commands, production deployment commands, troubleshooting guidance, security notes, and architecture documentation.

Generate the complete repository tree first, then provide every file in full. Ensure the application starts from a clean environment, initializes its database and artifact directories, validates dependencies, serves the frontend and API, executes a complete project pipeline, streams live progress, supports approval gates, produces a verified final export, and preserves a reproducible provenance record for every output.
```
